summary: In this episode, the hosts continue their exploration of apostolic succession, building on the previous discussion of Mosaic authority. They examine how Jesus Christ, while affirming the authority of the Pharisees who sat on Moses' seat, critiques their misuse of that authority and announces its transfer to the apostles. The episode delves into the nature of apostolic authority, its connection to the prophetic and priestly roles, and the establishment of a new chain of succession through the laying on of hands. The hosts also address the historical break in Jewish ordination, the development of the threefold ministry (bishop, presbyter, deacon), and the Orthodox understanding of primacy and conciliarity. They conclude with a discussion on the accountability of church leaders and the importance of obedience within the Church.

entities.title: Moses
entities.summary: The prophet and leader of Israel who received authority from God and passed it on through laying on of hands.

entities.title: Jesus Christ
entities.summary: The Son of God who affirms the authority of the Pharisees, critiques their misuse, and establishes a new chain of authority with the apostles.

entities.title: Pharisees
entities.summary: A Jewish religious party that held authority from Moses but were criticized by Jesus for hypocrisy and misuse of authority.

entities.title: Saint Peter
entities.summary: One of the apostles who received the keys of the kingdom and primacy among the apostles.

entities.title: Saint Paul
entities.summary: An apostle who was directly commissioned by Christ and appointed successors like Timothy and Titus.

entities.title: Joseph Smith
entities.summary: Founder of Mormonism who claimed to receive priesthood authority from angelic visitations, which the hosts contrast with apostolic succession.

concepts.title: Apostolic Succession
concepts.summary: The chain of authority passed from the apostles to their successors (bishops) through the laying on of hands, ensuring continuity of teaching and authority.

concepts.title: Seat of Moses
concepts.summary: The authority of the Pharisees to make authoritative rulings, which Jesus affirms while condemning their hypocrisy.

concepts.title: Laying on of Hands
concepts.summary: The physical ritual of ordination that conveys authority and grace, originating with Moses and continuing in the Church.

concepts.title: Primacy and Conciliarity
concepts.summary: The balance between individual authority (primacy) and collective decision-making (conciliarity) in the Church, as seen in the apostles and bishops.

concepts.title: Prophetic and Priestly Authority
concepts.summary: The distinction and recombination of prophetic (representing God to people) and priestly (representing people to God) roles in the apostolic office.

claims.text: Jesus affirmed that the Pharisees had legitimate authority from Moses, and his followers were to obey their rulings, even while criticizing their hypocrisy.
Christ gave the apostles the same authority to bind and loose, which they passed on through ordination to their successors.
The Jewish ordination chain from Moses ended between 360 and 425 AD, and modern rabbinical ordination is not the same as the ancient semikhah.
Bishops are accountable to God for their rulings, and the primary accountability is not to the laity but to God and the synod of bishops.

scriptural_links.summary: Jesus acknowledges the Pharisees sit on Moses' seat and instructs the crowds to obey their teachings.
Jesus gives Peter the keys of the kingdom and the authority to bind and loose.
Jesus gives the disciples authority to bind and loose in a conciliar context.
Jesus breathes on the apostles and gives them the Holy Spirit for the forgiveness of sins.
The Council of Jerusalem demonstrates the apostles exercising conciliar authority.
Paul reminds Timothy of the gift of God received through the laying on of hands.

glossary.definition: The Jewish practice of ordination through laying on of hands, which conveyed authority and grace.
Greek for 'overseer' or 'bishop', an office in the early church that succeeded the apostles.
Greek for 'elder', a term used for church leaders, often translated as 'priest'.
The principle of decision-making by councils of bishops, as opposed to a single authority.
